contentUnits.title: Hidden Attic
contentUnits.text: The fire started in the attic, a hidden, rarely visited space above Notre-Dame’s grand stone arches.

lifecycle.readerAction: Begin the guided sequence and look to the highlighted attic zone.
lifecycle.visualFocus: Lift the cathedral into a cutaway view and put the attic above the stone vaults at eye level.

contentUnits.title: Near The Spire
contentUnits.text: The source of the fire, likely near the spire, could have been an electrical problem or a human error, like a worker tossing a cigarette. It appeared to smolder out of sight for a time.

lifecycle.readerAction: Advance once the likely source area is clear.
lifecycle.visualFocus: Pull attention to the spire and the hidden ignition area where smoke could build out of sight.

contentUnits.title: Dry Wood Beams
contentUnits.text: The attic contained a combustible lattice of dry wood beams. Settled dust and debris could have made the area even more flammable.

lifecycle.readerAction: Follow the highlighted beam run from end to end.
lifecycle.visualFocus: Trace the combustible timber lattice as a continuous path under the roof.

contentUnits.title: Alarm Delay
contentUnits.text: When the first alarm went off at 6:20 p.m., no fire was found. By the time a second alarm sounded 23 minutes later, the flames were already racing across the beams.

lifecycle.readerAction: Compare the two alarms against the growing fire path.
lifecycle.visualFocus: Show the fire racing along the roofline after the first alarm did not locate it.

contentUnits.title: No Fire Walls
contentUnits.text: The cathedral had a smoke detection system, but not other basic fire-safety measures, such as fire-resistant walls that could have divided the space and helped to contain the fire.

lifecycle.readerAction: Notice how one open attic volume lets the fire travel.
lifecycle.visualFocus: Bring in ghosted partition planes to make the missing containment strategy legible.

contentUnits.title: Retrofit Gap
contentUnits.text: Other major cathedrals in Britain and France have been retrofitted with similar designs, but Notre-Dame was not.

lifecycle.readerAction: Read the comparison as a design choice, not a separate scene.
lifecycle.visualFocus: Hold the ghosted firewalls in view while the slide image frames the missed retrofit context.

contentUnits.title: No Sprinklers
contentUnits.text: Without firewalls, a sprinkler system could have slowed the fire. But the authorities had decided against one.

lifecycle.readerAction: Connect the absent system to the fire's speed.
lifecycle.visualFocus: Draw a blue sprinkler line above the attic to show the system that might have slowed the fire.

contentUnits.title: Roof And Spire
contentUnits.text: Images showed the fire tearing across the roof and up the spire, which eventually toppled.

lifecycle.readerAction: Watch the guided highlight peak at the spire.
lifecycle.visualFocus: Raise the flame effect across the roof and spire without moving the viewer uncomfortably.

contentUnits.title: Stone Ceiling
contentUnits.text: The architecture of the cathedral made fighting the fire difficult. The cathedral’s vaulted stone ceiling prevented firefighters from shooting water at the attic from the ground.

lifecycle.readerAction: Look below the attic to see why ground-level water could not reach the fire.
lifecycle.visualFocus: Show the stone vault as a protective barrier that also blocked water from the ground.

contentUnits.title: Fighting From Above
contentUnits.text: Instead, firefighters may have had to wait until the fire burned through the lead panels on the roof before they could start to spray water from above. Pulling hoses up winding staircases was also not an option.

lifecycle.readerAction: Keep your position and compare the above-roof water path with the blocked interior path.
lifecycle.visualFocus: Stage water from above after the roof gives way, with the stair constraint kept as narration.

contentUnits.title: Damage Over Time
contentUnits.text: After an inspection Tuesday, officials said the cathedral appeared structurally sound. But the damage may present itself over time: We don’t know what fire and water do to limestone quarried over 800 years ago.

lifecycle.readerAction: End with the uncertainty of fire and water damage to centuries-old stone.
lifecycle.visualFocus: Quiet the fire effects and leave the limestone and surviving structure in inspection light.
